passage:
Class teacher's note, Tuesday. Kiran Joshi, 9B.
At 11:40 Disha asked to see me in the empty lab. Her hands were shaking. Someone had posted a photo of her from sports day, mid-fall, in the class group, with cruel comments about her body. Forty-two people had reacted. She said, "Everyone's seen it. I want to change schools."
What I did: I told her clearly that this was not her fault, and that the people who posted and commented were in the wrong. We took screenshots together, with names and times, before anything could be deleted. She reported the post and blocked the two accounts, with me beside her. I called her mother at 12:15; she reached school by one. I informed the principal and the school counsellor the same afternoon, and the counsellor met Disha and her mother before home time. The photo was removed by 3 pm. Follow-up with Disha tomorrow at break.

qa.q: How many people had reacted to the post?
qa.a: Forty-two people had reacted.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she said she wanted to change schools?
qa.a: Disha felt exposed, humiliated and helpless, as her shaking hands and wish to escape show.

qa.q: Which practical steps did the teacher take with Disha?
qa.a: Saving screenshots with names and times, reporting and blocking together, calling her mother, and telling the principal and counsellor the same day.

qa.q: How might Disha's mother have felt getting the call?
qa.a: She was likely upset and worried, but also relieved that the school acted at once, which is why she reached school by one.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager shamed through a shared photo and cruel comments, and a teacher who says it is not her fault and helps her save evidence, report, block and tell adults the same day.

passage:
Tenzin's journal, Thursday, 1 am.
Scrolled for two hours. Rohit's in Bali. Urmila got the consulting job. Three weddings. Someone from school bought a car. I'm in my hostel room eating instant noodles, still waiting on two internship replies, and I felt like I'd been left on the platform while the train pulled out.
Then I remembered Urmila calling me last month, crying, because she'd been rejected six times before this job. None of that is on her page. Just the offer letter and a cake.
Everyone posts the cake. Nobody posts the six rejections.
New rule for me: phone goes in the drawer at eleven. No scrolling before breakfast. I moved the app off my home screen tonight.
Tomorrow I'll call Urmila and say congratulations properly, on the phone, not with a heart.
Also, I should sleep.

qa.q: What time does Tenzin's phone now go in the drawer?
qa.a: The phone goes in the drawer at eleven.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel while scrolling?
qa.a: Tenzin felt left behind and low, like being left on the platform while the train pulled out.

qa.q: What helped Tenzin see the posts differently?
qa.a: Remembering Urmila's six rejections behind one happy post showed that pages show only the highlights.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Tenzin calls to congratulate her properly?
qa.a: Urmila would probably feel warmly supported, since Tenzin knows the hard road behind the offer and not just the cake 😊

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who scrolls through friends' highlights and feels behind, then remembers that posts hide the hard parts and sets limits on phone time.

"Payal, did you forward this to the family group?" Kamal held up his phone: "Kidnappers in white vans taking children from school gates in our city."
"Yes! Bua's kids walk to school. People need to know."
"Where did it come from?"
"Mausi's friend sent it. It had a photo and everything."
"Look at the photo. That bus stop sign is in another language. And the city police page says there's no such case."
Payal's face went warm. "But it felt so important."
"That's how they're written. Chachi has already kept Anu home from school. Nani's crying."
"Oh no." Payal typed fast in the group: "Please ignore my last forward. I didn't check it. The police say it isn't true. Sorry, everyone."
"Good," Kamal said. "Next time, pause first. If you can't find where it came from, don't send it."

qa.q: Who had kept Anu home from school?
qa.a: Chachi had kept Anu home from school.

qa.q: Why did Payal forward the message in the first place?
qa.a: Payal was worried about Bua's kids and believed it was important, so fear pushed her to share without checking.

qa.q: What did Payal get right once she learnt the truth?
qa.a: She quickly posted a correction in the group, admitted she hadn't checked, pointed to the police and apologised.

qa.q: How might Nani have experienced the forward?
qa.a: Nani was frightened for the grandchildren and ended up crying, which shows how an unchecked rumour hurts real people.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who forwards a shocking message in a family group without checking, sees the harm, and learns to pause and check the source.

passage:
"Have you seen this?" Deepika turned her laptop. A shaky clip: a woman at a petrol pump shouting at a young attendant. "Two million views. Everyone's calling her a monster. Someone's posted her office address."
Yash watched it twice. His thumb hovered over the reply box. He had a line ready, something sharp and funny. "She does look awful," he said.
"Wait," Deepika said. "Someone's put up a longer version." In the longer clip, the attendant had splashed fuel on the woman's child's shoes and laughed. The woman still shouted too much. But it was a different story.
"So what now? Do we defend her?" Yash asked.
"We don't have to do anything. That's the point. She's getting threats over thirty seconds."
Yash deleted his line. "Feels strange to just not."
"It's the most useful thing we can do."

qa.q: How many views did the clip have?
qa.a: The clip had two million views.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling as his thumb hovered over the reply box?
qa.a: Yash felt the pull to join in, excited by a sharp, funny line and carried along by the crowd's anger.

qa.q: Why was deleting his line a quiet act of fairness?
qa.a: The longer clip showed the story was partial, and not adding to thousands of attacks avoided more cruelty toward someone already being threatened.

qa.q: How might the woman in the clip be experiencing the pile-on?
qa.a: She is likely frightened and overwhelmed, with her office address out and threats pouring in over thirty seconds of her worst moment.

grounding: It illustrates a user who watches a pile-on over a clip, feels the pull to join, sees the story is partial and refuses to add cruelty.

passage:
Aditi's journal, Sunday night.
Posted my "lessons from my first year as a product manager" slides today. Lots of likes, two recruiters in my inbox. I should feel great.
I don't, fully. Lesson 4 was "embrace failure", with a photo of me smiling at my desk. The actual failure was the launch in March, when I cried in the office bathroom. Nobody sees that version.
Every weekend now I think about what would make a good post instead of just living the weekend.
Lalit came over for dinner and said, "You told me more tonight than your whole page ever has." He meant it kindly. It stung anyway.
Decisions: I'll keep posting, it helps with work. But only true things, no fake glow. And the Sunday trek group, the dal I burn, Nani's calls: those stay off the internet. Some of me should just be mine.

qa.q: What was Lesson 4 in Aditi's post?
qa.a: Lesson 4 was "embrace failure".

qa.q: Why doesn't Aditi feel fully great about the likes?
qa.a: Aditi feels uneasy and a bit fake, because the smiling photo hides the day she cried in the office bathroom.

qa.q: What balance does Aditi decide on?
qa.a: Aditi will keep posting for work but only true things, and keep private parts of life, like the trek group and Nani's calls, off the internet.

qa.q: What might Lalit have meant by his comment at dinner?
qa.a: Lalit likely felt close to Aditi and wanted to gently point out that the real Aditi shows up in person, not on the page.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional who curates a public image, feels the strain of performing, and chooses honesty and private spaces to protect the self.

passage:
Dear Trisha,
You asked why I've been slow to reply lately. It's on purpose, and it's been good, so I wanted to explain properly instead of in a text.
In June I noticed I checked my phone before brushing my teeth and after switching off the light, and felt worse both times. So I made three small rules. No phone from 9 pm till breakfast; it charges in the kitchen. I muted about thirty accounts that left me feeling ugly or behind, including a few people I actually like. And every Saturday I meet someone in person, even just for chai.
I haven't quit anything. I still use the family group, the work chat, the recipe videos. I'm just the one deciding now.
I've read four books since June. I sleep before midnight. Could next Saturday be you?
Love,
Rukmini

qa.q: Where does Rukmini's phone charge at night?
qa.a: It charges in the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel checking the phone before brushing and after lights-out?
qa.a: Rukmini felt worse both times, uneasy and drained, which led to the new rules.

qa.q: Why do Rukmini's limits work without cutting off useful connection?
qa.a: They are small and specific, a phone-free window, muting draining accounts and weekly meet-ups, while keeping the family group, work chat and recipe videos.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Trisha would probably feel relieved that the slow replies weren't about Trisha, and warmly included by the Saturday invitation.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who sets phone-free times, mutes draining accounts and keeps real-life friendships without cutting off useful connection.

passage:
"Zeenat, in Istanbul every aunty in the market kissed Aditi's cheeks, and she giggled," Imran said, pushing the pram through the Oslo airport.
"Here nobody even touches her," Zeenat said. "Look." A woman smiled at Aditi from a polite distance. Aditi, just two, stared, then hid in Zeenat's scarf.
"Is she shy today?"
"No. She's watching me. When I'm relaxed, she's relaxed."
Zeenat smiled at the woman. Aditi peeped out, then waved.

qa.q: Where did every aunty in the market kiss Aditi's cheeks?
qa.a: In Istanbul, every aunty in the market kissed her cheeks.

qa.q: Why did Aditi peep out and wave after hiding?
qa.a: Aditi seemed to feel safe again once Zeenat smiled and relaxed, reading her mother's comfort.

qa.q: What helped Aditi feel at ease with a stranger?
qa.a: Zeenat staying relaxed and smiling at the woman showed Aditi it was safe to come out.

qa.q: How might the woman at the airport see her own behaviour?
qa.a: She was probably being kind in her own way, smiling from a polite distance because that is how warmth is shown where she lives.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler travelling abroad who meets very different touch norms and reads her parent's comfort to decide how to react.

passage:
"Dilnaz, look at me when I'm speaking," Ms. Madhuri said.
Dilnaz kept her eyes on the teacher's sandals. "Sorry, Miss."
"I'm not angry. I just want to know you're listening."
"I am listening. My Dadi says it's rude to stare at elders. You keep your eyes down to show respect."
Ms. Madhuri crouched so they were the same height. "Ah. So at home, eyes down means respect."
"Yes."
"In this classroom, eyes up means 'I'm with you'. Both are respectful. They just speak different languages."
Dilnaz peeked up, then down again. "Can I look at your nose? That's in between."
Ms. Madhuri laughed. "The nose is perfect. And at home, keep doing what Dadi taught you."

qa.q: Who told Dilnaz that staring at elders is rude?
qa.a: Her Dadi told her that.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when asked to look up?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt confused and a little anxious, caught between Dadi's rule and the teacher's request.

qa.q: What did Ms. Madhuri do well?
qa.a: She stayed calm, asked why, and translated between the two meanings instead of calling Dilnaz rude.

qa.q: How might Ms. Madhuri have first read Dilnaz's lowered eyes?
qa.a: At first the teacher may have wondered whether Dilnaz was listening, before learning that at home it signals respect.

grounding: It illustrates a child taught that eye contact with elders is rude who meets a teacher expecting it, and the patient translation between the two meanings.

passage:
Varun: ok culture shock of the day. asked my host sister if she wanted to come to the football match with us. she said "No, I don't like football." just like that 😳
Arnab: harsh
Varun: that's what I thought! but she wasn't angry. she offered to make pancakes for when we got back
Arnab: at home that'd be "let's see, maybe, I'll try" 😅
Varun: and then they don't come. exactly. and here if they say maybe, it means they're actually not sure
Arnab: so which is ruder?
Varun: neither I think. here the plain no is honest, at home the maybe is being polite. I kept hearing rude when it wasn't
Arnab: so what did you do
Varun: said "no problem, pancakes sound great." she smiled. and I'm practising a clear no myself
Arnab: try it on me. come to my cousin's engagement Sunday?
Varun: ...I'll see 🙂

qa.q: What did Varun's host sister offer to make?
qa.a: She offered to make pancakes for when they got back.

qa.q: What did Varun feel when his host sister said no so plainly?
qa.a: Varun felt surprised and a bit stung at first, hearing it as harsh before seeing she wasn't angry.

qa.q: What is Varun learning to do?
qa.a: Varun is learning to read both styles, not hearing rudeness in a plain no, and practising giving a clear no too.

qa.q: How might the host sister see her own "No, I don't like football"?
qa.a: To her it was probably just honest and friendly, which is why she offered pancakes right after.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager on an exchange who notices that people abroad say no bluntly while at home a no is softened, and learns that neither is rude in its own setting.

passage: In his first week at the lab in Copenhagen, Javier stood beside Ines at the coffee machine the way he would have in Bogota, shoulders almost touching, chatting warmly about the experiment. Ines took a step back. He stepped in again to keep talking. She stepped back again, until she was against the counter. That evening Javier sat in his flat feeling rejected. Maybe she didn't like him, or didn't like Colombians. On Friday the lab manager, Sofie, ran a short welcome session for new international staff and mentioned, between bike rules and lunch times, that people here often stand about an arm's length apart. Javier went red. On Monday at the machine he kept an arm's length. Ines talked for twenty minutes, asked about his family and invited him to Thursday's board-game night.

qa.q: How far apart did Sofie say people here often stand?
qa.a: About an arm's length apart.

qa.q: What did Javier feel that evening in his flat?
qa.a: Javier felt rejected and unsure, wondering whether Ines disliked him or Colombians.

qa.q: What basic courtesy did Javier learn to use?
qa.a: Noticing body language like stepping back, and adjusting his distance to local comfort, as he did on Monday.

qa.q: Why might Ines have kept stepping back?
qa.a: Ines was probably just uncomfortable with how close he stood, not rejecting him, as her warm talk on Monday shows.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult abroad who stands close to a colleague, feels rejected when she steps back, and later learns about different comfort distances and adjusts.
